Let the triangle have sides \(a,b,c\), semiperimeter \(s\), and area \(\Delta\). Define

\[
x=s-a,\qquad y=s-b,\qquad z=s-c.
\]

Then \(x,y,z>0\), and

\[
s=x+y+z,\qquad a=y+z,\quad b=z+x,\quad c=x+y.
\]

Using the standard area formulas for the incircle and excircles,

\[
\Delta=rs=r_a(s-a)=r_b(s-b)=r_c(s-c),
\]

so

\[
r=\frac{\Delta}{s},\qquad r_a=\frac{\Delta}{x},\qquad r_b=\frac{\Delta}{y},\qquad r_c=\frac{\Delta}{z}.
\]

Thus the four radii are a positive multiple of the reciprocals of

\[
s,x,y,z.
\]

Taking reciprocals of a geometric progression gives another geometric progression (in reverse order), so the four numbers \(s,x,y,z\) can also be arranged as consecutive terms of a geometric progression.

Since

\[
s=x+y+z,
\]

we have \(s>x,y,z\). Therefore, when the four numbers are arranged in increasing order, \(s\) must be the largest term. Let the common ratio be \(q>1\). Then, up to order,

\[
x=p,\qquad y=pq,\qquad z=pq^2
\]

for some \(p>0\), and

\[
s=pq^3.
\]

But also

\[
s=x+y+z=p(1+q+q^2).
\]

Hence

\[
pq^3=p(1+q+q^2),
\]

so

\[
q^3=q^2+q+1. \tag{1}
\]

Now the side lengths of the triangle are the pairwise sums of \(x,y,z\). Up to order, they are

\[
p(1+q),\qquad p(1+q^2),\qquad p(q+q^2).
\]

The largest side is

\[
L=p(q+q^2).
\]

Let \(\theta\) be the angle opposite this largest side. By the Law of Cosines,

\[
\cos\theta
=
\frac{p^2(1+q)^2+p^2(1+q^2)^2-p^2(q+q^2)^2}
{2p^2(1+q)(1+q^2)}.
\]

Canceling \(p^2\), the numerator is

\[
(1+q)^2+(1+q^2)^2-(q+q^2)^2.
\]

Expanding,

\[
(1+2q+q^2)+(1+2q^2+q^4)-(q^2+2q^3+q^4)
\]

\[
=2+2q+2q^2-2q^3
=2(1+q+q^2-q^3).
\]

By (1), \(1+q+q^2-q^3=0\). Therefore,

\[
\cos\theta=0,
\]

so

\[
\theta=90^\circ.
\]

Since \(\theta\) is opposite the largest side, it is the largest angle of the triangle.

\[
\boxed{90^\circ}
\]
